name: ABL Landscape Architecture
description: ABL Landscape Architecture is an award-winning, client-focused landscape architecture firm based in Lexington, Virginia offering expertise in institutional, civic, residential and commercial landscape architecture projects.
statement: ABL Landscape Architecture is principally devoted to the adaptation of historic, environmentally sensitive landscapes to contemporary needs and goals.

intro: The firm seeks to distill the essence of a site, and to respond to its innate character and context with creative, enduring design. ABL assists clients through all phases from initial concept to landscape establishment and maturation. We embrace open dialogue and exploration with clients, allied professionals, contractors, and end-users.

Mindful of the client's need to visualize the final product and also of the client's cost constraints in landscape construction and maintenance, ABL seeks every reasonable means to narrow the uncertainty between design incubation and the desired outcome. Such techniques include photo simulation, 3D scale models, material samples, full scale mock-ups, detailed review of pricing, dialogue with both grounds staff and end-users, and frequent site visits.
studio.note: ABL is a SWaM certified small business.

intro: ABL is a practice of three. A client's first conversation is with the people who will study the site, prepare the drawings and remain with the work, alongside the contractor, until it is built; no part of a commission passes to staff the client has not met.

Decades of practice in Lexington and Rockbridge County have given the firm a working knowledge of the place: its contractors, the plants that establish well in its soils, and the boards and offices through which a project must pass. Arthur Bartenstein serves on the City of Lexington's Tree Committee and its Architectural Review Board. Kelly Morikawa, a certified arborist, owned and operated a landscape design, installation and maintenance company in the area for eighteen years and knows how a drawing becomes built work.

The firm approaches a site as a preservationist would, by learning first how the ground came to its present form and what was intended for it. New work is then designed to be, in Arthur Bartenstein's phrase, "registered in terms of place, but also registered in terms of time": fitted to what surrounds it and candid about its own date. Each design is tested before it is built, in photo simulations, scale models and material samples and in full-scale mock-ups on the site, and it is developed throughout with the client, with the architects and engineers on the project, and with the people who will use and maintain the grounds.

The work ranges from private gardens to the Virginia Horse Center and the campuses of Washington and Lee University and the Virginia Military Institute. Before founding ABL, Arthur Bartenstein practiced with Peter Walker and Partners and the SWA Group in California and with Hill Studio in Roanoke and Frazier Associates in Staunton, on projects in Florida, California, Northern Virginia, Japan and China.

text: Arthur Bartenstein draws every commission as a triangle whose corners are the client, the site and the design team, with arrows running between them. The client states what is wanted; the site, once those wishes are tested against it, determines part of the answer; and a scheme that fails on the ground returns to the client for another conversation. The arrows are that dialogue, and the design is its result.

process.stepsIntro: No two commissions proceed alike, but each begins with the same three steps, and at every stage the client is told where the work stands.

steps.title: First meeting
steps.text: The work begins on the property, in conversation with the client about what is wanted of the place, how it is used, what has failed, and what budget is available.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: Before anything is drawn, the firm studies the land itself and the history of the property and of the area around it.

steps.title: Brainstorming and mock-ups
steps.text: Ideas are worked out with the client in sketches and models, and the chosen scheme is mocked up at full scale on the site before construction begins, so that the client sees the result in place while it can still be changed.

services.intro: Every commission, whatever its size, receives the same research and the same attention through construction. For a house, a garden or a farm, the firm is most often engaged in one of four ways.
services.reviewNote: Service descriptions drafted by Claude from the November 11 meeting and rewritten the same day. The firm to confirm the scope of each and the wording.

items.name: Consultation
items.text: A visit to the property and a conversation about what it could become, concluding in recommendations the owner can act upon.

items.name: Planting plan
items.text: A plan of what to plant and where, prepared for the property's soil, light and upkeep by people who know which plants establish well in this region.

items.name: Master plan
items.text: A complete design for the property: research, the plan itself, drawings from which a contractor can build, and the firm's involvement until the work is finished.

items.name: Single elements
items.text: One part of a property, a stair for example, designed and seen through construction.

work.intro: Campus, civic and preservation commissions in Lexington, Rockbridge County and elsewhere in Virginia: built work, shown with the plans and studies that precede it.
